content.title: A first-timer’s guide to Joshua Tree National Park, where trees and rocks compete for attention
content.text: JOSHUA TREE, California – The trees here get all the glory. But the rocks may be the coolest part of Joshua Tree National Park.Don’t get me wrong – the trees are also special, with their Seuss-like branches and spiky leaves.But you can’t climb the trees.The rocks, on the other hand, are open for exploration.Unlike some national parks, where visitors are discouraged from getting too close, explorers here are encouraged to hike, scramble, climb up, rappel down and otherwise fully experience the hundreds of igneous rock formations that dot the landscape.I skipped the rappelling part, but otherwise tested my knees and rewarded my eyes by hiking in and around the boulder piles, through stands of trees and alongside bursts of blooming wildflowers during my inaugural trip to Joshua Tree last month.At nearly 800,000 acres – about the size of Rhode Island – the park is large enough to fill a weekend or more, but small enough to explore in a day.Located about 130 miles east of Los Angeles, the park can get very busy on weekends. On the Saturday morning of my visit, there was a line of cars waiting at the entrance booth to get into the park, so time your visit during the week if possible.Once inside, I found myself competing for space with a youth group of trail runners on the Hidden Valley path, one of the most popular in the park.But the crowds dispersed after that and it didn’t feel busy again until we all gathered for sunset at Keys View.Related: Sauna to snowball fight in minutes: Palm Springs tramway delivers a cool escape above the heatAt Skull Rock, one of numerous named rocks inside Joshua Tree National Park.Susan Glaser, Cleveland.comA crowd gathers for sunset at Keys View in Joshua Tree National Park.Susan Glaser, Cleveland.comHiking the trail to Fortynine Palms Oasis in Joshua Trail.Susan Glaser, Cleveland.comExploring Joshua TreeThe park takes its name from the distinctive Joshua trees that dot the landscape, native to the areas in and around the Mojave Desert, which spans southeastern California and extends into Nevada, Arizona and Utah.The trees were named by 19th century Mormon settlers who believed the plant’s outstretched branches resembled the biblical figure Joshua reaching up to the sky, guiding them westward.Pop music fans may know the plant best from the Irish band U2, whose bestselling 1987 album, “The Joshua Tree,” evokes a search for meaning in a “spiritual desert,” according to critics.My own search in this desert was more practical: water. There are precious few places to refill a water bottle inside the park and the desert sun is unrelenting. So come prepared.Joshua Tree has no overnight lodge, no restaurants within park boundaries. There are five campgrounds, most of which offer only pit toilets and no water.The majority of overnight visitors stay in one of a handful of gateway towns immediately north of the park boundary. We stayed in the small town of Joshua Tree, a five minute drive from the park entrance.Rock climbing at Joshua Tree National Park; this is on the Hidden Valley Trail.Susan Glaser, Cleveland.comThe Cholla Cactus Garden, in the eastern half of Joshua Tree, is part of the Colorado Desert, which is hotter and drier than the Mojave.Susan Glaser, Cleveland.comThe Fortynine Palms Oasis is one of five fan palm oases within the park, fed by underground springs; this one is accessed via the Fortynine Palms Trail.Susan Glaser, Cleveland.comHiking highlightsLike most national parks, Joshua Tree offers a range of experiences for a variety of interests and fitness levels, from scenic drives to demanding hikes, stunning overlooks and relaxing strolls.The park’s main road, Park Boulevard, connects the West and North entrances and passes many of the park’s top attractions, including Hidden Valley, Skull Rock and Split Rock.With more than 300 miles of trails, it’s impossible to see everything in one visit. We opted for several shorter hikes to experience a variety of terrain.Among the highlights: the 1.1-mile Barker Dam Nature Trail, which leads to a small dam built by cattle ranchers in the early 20th-century, before the area became a protected national monument in 1936.For a deeper look at early settler life, visitors can tour Keys Ranch, where the Keys family farmed for five decades before the property was acquired by the park service. (Reservations are required and should be made in advance at recreation.gov.)We also hiked the 1.7-mile Skull Rock Trail, winding through and around dozens of rock formations, including one with hollowed out eyes that resembles a skull.Other rocks have fun names too – from Heart Rock to the Great Burrito to the Hall of Horrors.All of the park’s Joshua trees and most of the rock formations are concentrated in the park’s northern and western regions. In the southeast, the landscape transitions into the Colorado Desert, which is lower, hotter and more barren than the Mojave.Our main stop here was the Cholla Cactus Garden, a 10-acre patch of “teddy bear” cholla, nicknamed “jumping cactus” because of the way its spiny segments can stick to clothing and skin. I swapped my hiking sandals for boots on this one.My favorite hike of the trip was 49 Palms Oasis, a 3.5-mile moderately strenuous out and back trail with a terrific payoff: a lush grove of California fan palms, one of a handful in the park.These oases require a constant supply of water and typically appear along fault lines, where underground water is pushed to the surface.For one final Joshua Tree adventure, we headed south through the park to Keys View, elevation 5,185 feet, a popular spot to witness the park’s signature lavender sunsets.From here, you can see west toward Palm Springs and the Coachella Valley, and south toward the Salton Sea, California’s largest lake.Look closely and you can also make out the San Andreas Fault, a major fracture in the Earth’s crust that is responsible for thousands of small earthquakes every year. A sign at the overlook offered this less-than-comforting detail: “There has not been a big earthquake in this segment of the San Andreas Fault for over 300 years. The Coachella Valley is overdue for a major earthquake.”With that, we bid farewell to Joshua Tree.We considered staying for stargazing – Joshua Tree was designated an International Dark Sky Park in 2017 - but a bright moon and empty stomachs sent us back toward town.As we headed down the mountain at dusk, we drove past more fantastical trees growing alongside equally impressive rock formations, where a couple of climbers with headlamps were just getting started.Joshua Tree National Park is named after the tree that grows in abundance here and elsewhere in and near the Mojave Desert.Susan Glaser, Cleveland.comRocks galore on the Hidden Valley Trail at Joshua Tree.Susan Glaser, Cleveland.comSunset in the desert; at Joshua Tree National Park in California.Susan Glaser, Cleveland.comIf you go: Joshua Tree National ParkWhat: Joshua Tree attracted 2.93 million visitors in 2025, the nation’s 12th most-visited park (just behind Northeast Ohio’s Cuyahoga Valley). It’s located about 130 miles from Los Angeles, 160 miles from San Diego and 220 miles from Las Vegas.Related: These were the most visited national parks in 2025When: The park is open year-round but can be brutally hot in the summer, when high temperatures routinely exceed 100 degrees. Spring and fall are the most popular times to explore, with more moderate temperatures. Winters can get cold at night, with snow possible in higher elevations.Admission: A seven-day per-vehicle park pass is $30, or buy an $80 annual pass that’s good at National Park Service sites across the U.S.Where to stay: There are five campgrounds inside the park, most of which offer pit toilets with no running water. Most overnight visitors stay in one of several towns bordering the park, including Joshua Tree, Yucca Valley and Twentynine Palms. Palm Springs is about an hour away.We spent two nights at the well-located but modest Joshua Tree Inn. The inn received some notoriety decades ago, after musician Gram Parsons overdosed here in 1973. The hotel does not shy away from this fact, proclaiming to be “The Home of Gram Parsons’ Spirit,” according to a sign in the lobby. We paid about $175 per night.Where to eat: We enjoyed meals at Crossroads Café and JT Country Kitchen. We tried to eat at Pappy and Harriet’s - a popular barbecue joint and live music venue in Pioneertown, an old movie set with shops and restaurants – but the wait was over two hours. Maybe next time.Nearby: On our way out of town, we stopped at the Noah Purifoy Outdoor Desert Art Museum, filled with creations from the late visionary artist. Purifoy, who died in 2004, was a pioneer in using discarded objects in his work – including old toilets, tires, clothing, dishware and more. Many of his works appear in top museums, including the Museum of Modern Art and the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York City. The museum, located at his former studio just north of town, is open daylight hours and is free.
